# The sequence $\delta_n(x)=\dfrac n\pi\,\dfrac1{1+n^2x^2}$ is a delta sequence

## 0. Statement, notation and what has to be proved

Throughout, $\mathcal D(\mathbb R)$ denotes the space of **test functions**: the set of all
$\varphi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ that are infinitely differentiable and have compact support.
A **Schwartz distribution** is a continuous linear functional $T:\mathcal D(\mathbb R)\to\mathbb C$,
and the **Dirac delta distribution** $\delta$ is the distribution defined by

$$\delta(\varphi):=\varphi(0),\qquad \varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R).$$

Every locally integrable function $f$ on $\mathbb R$ induces a distribution $T_f$, the *regular
distribution* associated with $f$, by

$$T_f(\varphi):=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,\varphi(x)\,\mathrm dx ,\qquad \varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R),$$

the integral being over the (compact) support of $\varphi$, hence finite. That $T_f$ is indeed a
distribution is standard: it is clearly linear, and if $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq K$ for a
compact $K$ then $\lvert T_f(\varphi)\rvert\le\bigl(\int_K\lvert f\rvert\bigr)\sup_{\mathbb R}\lvert\varphi\rvert$,
which is the required continuity estimate on the test functions supported in $K$. Likewise
$\delta$ is a distribution, since $\lvert\delta(\varphi)\rvert=\lvert\varphi(0)\rvert\le\sup_{\mathbb R}\lvert\varphi\rvert$.
Convergence $T_n\to T$ in the space $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R)$ of distributions is, by definition,
pointwise convergence of the functionals: $T_n(\varphi)\to T(\varphi)$ for every
$\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R)$.

A sequence $(f_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_{>0}}$ of locally integrable functions is a **delta sequence** if
$T_{f_n}\to\delta$ in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R)$.

For $n\in\mathbb N_{>0}$ put

$$\delta_n(x):=\frac n\pi\,\frac1{1+n^2x^2},\qquad x\in\mathbb R .$$

**Theorem.** $(\delta_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_{>0}}$ is a delta sequence. Explicitly, for every test
function $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R)$,

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac n\pi\,\frac{\varphi(x)}{1+n^2x^2}\,\mathrm dx=\varphi(0)=\delta(\varphi).$$

The formula "$\lim_{n\to\infty}\delta_n(x)=\delta(x)$" appearing in the statement of the problem is
the usual abuse of notation for exactly this assertion; it is *not* a statement about pointwise
limits of functions (see Remark 3 in §5, where the genuine pointwise limit is computed and shown to
be $0$ almost everywhere).

All integrals below are Lebesgue integrals. Since every integrand occurring is continuous, and since
for nonnegative continuous integrands the Lebesgue integral over $\mathbb R$ coincides with the
improper Riemann integral $\lim_{A,B\to\infty}\int_{-A}^{B}$ (monotone convergence applied to the
increasing sequence of truncations), the elementary computations with antiderivatives made below are
legitimate.

## 1. Elementary properties of $\delta_n$

**Lemma 1.** For each $n\in\mathbb N_{>0}$ the function $\delta_n$ is well defined, strictly
positive, infinitely differentiable on $\mathbb R$, and

$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\,\mathrm dx=1 .$$

In particular each $\delta_n$ is integrable on $\mathbb R$, hence locally integrable, so the regular
distribution $T_{\delta_n}$ is defined.

*Proof.* For every real $x$ we have $1+n^2x^2\ge 1>0$, so the quotient is defined and positive, and
$x\mapsto \frac n\pi (1+n^2x^2)^{-1}$ is a quotient of polynomials with nowhere-vanishing
denominator, hence is $C^\infty$ (in particular continuous and Lebesgue measurable).

For the integral, fix $n\ge 1$ and $0<A<\infty$. The function $x\mapsto \frac1\pi\arctan(nx)$ is
differentiable with derivative
$$\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\Big(\frac1\pi\arctan (nx)\Big)=\frac1\pi\cdot\frac{n}{1+n^2x^2}=\delta_n(x),$$
so by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
$$\int_{-A}^{A}\delta_n(x)\,\mathrm dx=\frac1\pi\bigl(\arctan(nA)-\arctan(-nA)\bigr)=\frac2\pi\arctan(nA).$$
As $A\to\infty$ we have $nA\to\infty$ and $\arctan(nA)\to\frac\pi2$, so
$\int_{-A}^{A}\delta_n\to 1$. Since $\delta_n\ge0$, the monotone convergence theorem applied to
$\delta_n\mathbf 1_{[-A,A]}\uparrow\delta_n$ (as $A\to\infty$ through any increasing sequence) gives
$\int_{\mathbb R}\delta_n=1$. $\blacksquare$

Taking $n=1$ in Lemma 1 records the normalisation that will be used repeatedly:

$$\frac1\pi\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm dt}{1+t^2}=1. \tag{1.1}$$

**Lemma 2 (tail bound).** For every $R>0$,
$$\frac1\pi\int_{\lvert t\rvert>R}\frac{\mathrm dt}{1+t^2}
=\frac2\pi\Bigl(\frac\pi2-\arctan R\Bigr)\xrightarrow[R\to\infty]{}0 ,$$
and moreover $\displaystyle\frac1\pi\int_{\lvert t\rvert>R}\frac{\mathrm dt}{1+t^2}\le\frac{2}{\pi R}$.

*Proof.* By the computation in Lemma 1 with $n=1$,
$\frac1\pi\int_{-A}^{A}\frac{\mathrm dt}{1+t^2}=\frac2\pi\arctan A$, and letting $A\to\infty$ and
subtracting $\frac1\pi\int_{-R}^{R}=\frac2\pi\arctan R$ from $(1.1)$ gives the stated equality;
$\arctan R\to\frac\pi2$ as $R\to\infty$ yields the limit. For the quantitative bound, use
$1+t^2\ge t^2$ to get
$\int_{|t|>R}\frac{\mathrm dt}{1+t^2}\le 2\int_R^\infty \frac{\mathrm dt}{t^2}=\frac2R$. $\blacksquare$

## 2. $T_{\delta_n}(\varphi)$ is an absolutely convergent integral

Let $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R)$. Being continuous with compact support, $\varphi$ is bounded;
set
$$M:=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}\lvert\varphi(x)\rvert<\infty .$$
Then $\lvert\delta_n\varphi\rvert\le M\,\delta_n$ pointwise, and $\int_{\mathbb R}M\delta_n=M<\infty$
by Lemma 1. Hence $\delta_n\varphi\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ and
$$I_n:=T_{\delta_n}(\varphi)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\varphi(x)\,\mathrm dx$$
is a well-defined (absolutely convergent) integral for every $n$. (Of course $\varphi$ has compact
support, so this is really an integral over a bounded interval; the above remark shows in addition
that the same expression makes sense for any bounded continuous $\varphi$, which is used in
Remark 2.)

## 3. The scaling substitution

**Lemma 3.** For every $n\in\mathbb N_{>0}$ and every $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R)$,
$$I_n=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac n\pi\,\frac{\varphi(x)}{1+n^2x^2}\,\mathrm dx
=\frac1\pi\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\varphi(t/n)}{1+t^2}\,\mathrm dt . \tag{3.1}$$

*Proof.* The map $\Phi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $\Phi(t)=t/n$, is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of
$\mathbb R$ onto $\mathbb R$ (it is linear and bijective because $n\ne0$) with constant derivative
$\Phi'(t)=1/n>0$. The integrand $x\mapsto\delta_n(x)\varphi(x)$ is in $L^1(\mathbb R)$ by §2, so the
change-of-variables formula for Lebesgue integrals under a $C^1$ diffeomorphism applies and gives
$$\int_{\mathbb R}\delta_n(x)\varphi(x)\,\mathrm dx
=\int_{\mathbb R}\delta_n\bigl(\Phi(t)\bigr)\varphi\bigl(\Phi(t)\bigr)\,\lvert\Phi'(t)\rvert\,\mathrm dt
=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac n\pi\cdot\frac{1}{1+n^2(t/n)^2}\cdot\varphi(t/n)\cdot\frac1n\,\mathrm dt .$$
Since $n^2(t/n)^2=t^2$ and $\frac n\pi\cdot\frac1n=\frac1\pi$, this is exactly the right-hand side of
$(3.1)$. $\blacksquare$

(Equivalently, and without invoking the general change-of-variables theorem: on each bounded interval
the substitution $x=t/n$ in the Riemann integral $\int_{-A}^{A}$ is the elementary substitution rule,
and one passes to the limit $A\to\infty$ using absolute convergence.)

## 4. Proof of the Theorem

Let $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R)$ and let $M=\sup_{\mathbb R}\lvert\varphi\rvert<\infty$ as in §2.
By Lemma 3 and by the normalisation $(1.1)$ (which lets us write
$\varphi(0)=\frac1\pi\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\varphi(0)}{1+t^2}\,\mathrm dt$, an absolutely convergent
integral), we may subtract the two convergent integrals termwise:

$$I_n-\varphi(0)=\frac1\pi\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\varphi(t/n)-\varphi(0)}{1+t^2}\,\mathrm dt . \tag{4.1}$$

Hence
$$\bigl\lvert I_n-\varphi(0)\bigr\rvert\le\frac1\pi\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\lvert\varphi(t/n)-\varphi(0)\rvert}{1+t^2}\,\mathrm dt . \tag{4.2}$$

Now let $\varepsilon>0$ be given.

**Choice of $R$ (control of the tail).** Since $\lvert\varphi(t/n)-\varphi(0)\rvert\le 2M$ for all
$t$ and all $n$, Lemma 2 allows us to pick $R>0$ so large that
$$\frac{2M+1}{\pi}\int_{\lvert t\rvert>R}\frac{\mathrm dt}{1+t^2}<\frac\varepsilon2 ; \tag{4.3}$$
indeed the left-hand side tends to $0$ as $R\to\infty$. (The harmless summand $+1$ makes the choice
legitimate also in the degenerate case $M=0$.) Consequently, for every $n$,
$$\frac1\pi\int_{\lvert t\rvert>R}\frac{\lvert\varphi(t/n)-\varphi(0)\rvert}{1+t^2}\,\mathrm dt
\le\frac{2M}{\pi}\int_{\lvert t\rvert>R}\frac{\mathrm dt}{1+t^2}<\frac\varepsilon2 . \tag{4.4}$$

**Choice of $N$ (control of the central part).** The function $\varphi$ is continuous at $0$, so
there is $\eta>0$ such that
$$\lvert u\rvert<\eta\ \Longrightarrow\ \lvert\varphi(u)-\varphi(0)\rvert<\frac\varepsilon2 . \tag{4.5}$$
Choose $N\in\mathbb N_{>0}$ with $N>R/\eta$. Let $n\ge N$ and $\lvert t\rvert\le R$. Then
$$\Bigl\lvert\frac tn\Bigr\rvert\le\frac Rn\le\frac RN<\eta ,$$
so $(4.5)$ gives $\lvert\varphi(t/n)-\varphi(0)\rvert<\varepsilon/2$. Therefore, for $n\ge N$,
$$\frac1\pi\int_{\lvert t\rvert\le R}\frac{\lvert\varphi(t/n)-\varphi(0)\rvert}{1+t^2}\,\mathrm dt
\le\frac\varepsilon2\cdot\frac1\pi\int_{\lvert t\rvert\le R}\frac{\mathrm dt}{1+t^2}
\le\frac\varepsilon2\cdot\frac1\pi\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm dt}{1+t^2}
=\frac\varepsilon2 , \tag{4.6}$$
the last equality being $(1.1)$.

**Conclusion.** Splitting the integral in $(4.2)$ over $\{\lvert t\rvert\le R\}$ and
$\{\lvert t\rvert>R\}$ (legitimate: the integrand is nonnegative and integrable, being bounded by
$2M/(1+t^2)$), and combining $(4.4)$ and $(4.6)$, we obtain for all $n\ge N$
$$\bigl\lvert I_n-\varphi(0)\bigr\rvert<\frac\varepsilon2+\frac\varepsilon2=\varepsilon .$$

As $\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary, $\lim_{n\to\infty}I_n=\varphi(0)=\delta(\varphi)$.

Since $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R)$ was arbitrary, $T_{\delta_n}(\varphi)\to\delta(\varphi)$ for
every test function, i.e. $T_{\delta_n}\to\delta$ in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R)$. Together with
Lemma 1 (each $\delta_n$ is locally integrable, so $T_{\delta_n}$ is indeed a distribution), this
says precisely that $(\delta_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_{>0}}$ is a delta sequence. $\blacksquare$

## 5. Remarks

**Remark 1 (alternative ending by dominated convergence).** Instead of the $\varepsilon$-argument of
§4 one may argue as follows from $(3.1)$. Put $g_n(t):=\dfrac{\varphi(t/n)}{1+t^2}$. Each $g_n$ is
continuous, hence measurable; for every fixed $t$ we have $t/n\to0$ and $\varphi$ is continuous, so
$g_n(t)\to\dfrac{\varphi(0)}{1+t^2}$; and $\lvert g_n(t)\rvert\le\dfrac{M}{1+t^2}$, which is
integrable by $(1.1)$. The dominated convergence theorem therefore yields
$$I_n=\frac1\pi\int_{\mathbb R}g_n(t)\,\mathrm dt\ \longrightarrow\ \frac1\pi\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\varphi(0)}{1+t^2}\,\mathrm dt=\varphi(0).$$
The argument in §4 is a self-contained proof of exactly this instance of dominated convergence.

**Remark 2 (what was actually used).** The proof used only that $\varphi$ is bounded, measurable and
continuous at $0$; smoothness and compactness of the support were never needed. Hence the stronger
statement holds: for every bounded measurable $\varphi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ that is continuous at
$0$,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac n\pi\frac{\varphi(x)}{1+n^2x^2}\,\mathrm dx=\varphi(0).$$
In particular the conclusion holds for all $\varphi$ in the Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$ and
for all bounded continuous $\varphi$, not merely for $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R)$. The same
proof, verbatim, works with the discrete parameter $n\in\mathbb N_{>0}$ replaced by a continuous
parameter $\lambda\to\infty$.

**Remark 3 (the limit is not a function).** For fixed $x\ne0$ we have
$\delta_n(x)=\frac n\pi\frac1{1+n^2x^2}\le\frac{n}{\pi n^2x^2}=\frac1{\pi n x^2}\to0$, while
$\delta_n(0)=n/\pi\to\infty$. So the pointwise limit of $\delta_n$ is $0$ for every $x\neq 0$ and
$+\infty$ at $x=0$; in particular the pointwise limit is $0$ almost everywhere, whose associated
regular distribution is the zero distribution, not $\delta$. This is why the limit in the theorem
must be understood in the distributional sense and why "$\delta(x)$" is only an abuse of notation.
It also shows that for $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R)$ with $\varphi(0)\ne0$ there is **no**
integrable $g$ with $\lvert\delta_n\varphi\rvert\le g$ for all $n$: such a $g$ would, by the dominated
convergence theorem, force $\int\delta_n\varphi\to\int\lim_n(\delta_n\varphi)=0$, contradicting the
Theorem. In other words, the mass of $\delta_n$ escapes into an ever-narrower spike at the origin
while the total area stays equal to $1$ — the graphs become "thinner and taller", as the picture
accompanying the statement indicates. (This is not in conflict with Remark 1: there the dominated
convergence theorem is applied *after* the rescaling $(3.1)$, to the family $g_n$, which does admit
the integrable dominating function $M/(1+t^2)$.)

**Remark 4 (rate of convergence).** For $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R)$ one gets a quantitative
version. Let $K:=\sup_{\mathbb R}\lvert\varphi'\rvert<\infty$ (finite since $\varphi'$ is continuous
with compact support). From the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus,
$\varphi(u)-\varphi(0)=\int_0^u\varphi'(s)\,\mathrm ds$, whence
$\lvert\varphi(u)-\varphi(0)\rvert\le K\lvert u\rvert$ for all $u\in\mathbb R$ (this is valid for
complex-valued $\varphi$ as well, by the standard estimate
$\lvert\int_0^u h\rvert\le\lvert\int_0^u\lvert h\rvert\rvert$); also
$\lvert\varphi(u)-\varphi(0)\rvert\le 2M$ always. Splitting $(4.2)$ at $\lvert t\rvert=n$ and using
these two bounds on the respective pieces,
$$\frac1\pi\int_{\lvert t\rvert\le n}\frac{K\lvert t\rvert/n}{1+t^2}\,\mathrm dt
=\frac{2K}{\pi n}\int_0^n\frac{t\,\mathrm dt}{1+t^2}=\frac{K\ln(1+n^2)}{\pi n},$$
$$\frac1\pi\int_{\lvert t\rvert>n}\frac{2M}{1+t^2}\,\mathrm dt\le\frac{4M}{\pi n}$$
(the latter by Lemma 2), whence
$$\bigl\lvert I_n-\varphi(0)\bigr\rvert\le\frac{K\ln(1+n^2)}{\pi n}+\frac{4M}{\pi n}=O\!\left(\frac{\ln n}{n}\right).$$
The logarithm is genuinely present and reflects the heavy $1/t^2$ tail of the Cauchy kernel: unlike,
say, the Gaussian delta sequence, $\delta_n$ has no finite first absolute moment.
